faq.q: Is Kaomoji Copy free to use?
faq.a: Yes. Every face is free to copy and paste, and there is nothing to sign up for.

faq.q: How do I copy a kaomoji?
faq.a: Tap or click any face. It is copied to your clipboard and a small message confirms it. Then paste it where you want it, with Ctrl+V on a computer or by long-pressing and choosing Paste on a phone.

faq.q: What is the difference between kaomoji and emoji?
faq.a: Emoji are small pictures. Kaomoji are faces built from ordinary text characters and symbols, and they are read upright instead of tilted on their side like :-).
In your own browser, on the device you are using. There is no account, so favorites do not follow you to another device, and clearing your browser data removes them.

faq.q: Why does a face look different or show empty boxes on my device?
faq.a: Kaomoji use many different symbols, and each phone or computer draws them with its own fonts. If a symbol is missing from your device's fonts, it can look slightly different or show as a box. Another face from the same collection usually works fine.

faq.q: Can I use kaomoji on my phone?
faq.a: Yes. The site works on iPhone, Android, and desktop browsers. Tap a face to copy it, then paste it into any app that accepts text.
Kaomoji is a Japanese word that combines kao, meaning face, and moji, meaning character. It describes faces built from text characters, such as (˶ᵔ ᵕ ᵔ˶).

faq.q: Is it kaomoji, kaomojis or kamoji?
faq.a: Kaomoji is the correct spelling and can be used for one face or many. Kaomojis is a common English plural, and kamoji is a frequent misspelling. All of them lead to the same kind of text faces.

faq.q: What are the best kaomoji for Instagram and TikTok?
faq.a: Cute, aesthetic, and happy kaomoji are the most popular for bios, captions, and comments. Copy one, paste it, and keep it short so it stays easy to read.

faq.q: Are kaomoji the same as ASCII art?
faq.a: They are related. ASCII art uses text characters to make pictures, and kaomoji are very small pictures of faces. Kaomoji are usually one line long and meant to be sent in messages.

faq.q: Can I make my own kaomoji?
faq.a: Yes. Combine characters you like for the eyes, mouth, and arms, and test the result in your app. You can start by copying a face from the library and changing one part.

sections.h: Kaomoji, kaomojis and kamoji: which spelling is right?
sections.p:
The standard spelling is kaomoji, and it works for one face or many. Plenty of people write kaomojis with an English plural, and some type kamoji by mistake. They all mean the same thing: Japanese-style faces made from text. If you searched for any of these spellings, you are in the right place.

The word comes from Japanese. Kao means face and moji means character, so kaomoji literally means face characters. You can read more in our guide, [what is kaomoji](/what-is-kaomoji.html).

sections.h: Kaomoji, emoticons and emoji: what is the difference?
sections.p:
Western emoticons such as :) are read sideways, and emoji are small pictures that look different on each device. Kaomoji are Japanese emoticons that you read upright, and they put most of the feeling in the eyes, like (ᵔ◡ᵔ). Because kaomoji are plain text, they paste the same way everywhere.

For a deeper comparison, including ASCII art and symbols, see [Japanese emoticons explained](/japanese-emoticons.html).

sections.h: Find the right kaomoji for your message
sections.p:
Start with the mood. [Cute kaomoji](/kaomoji/cute.html) are best for soft, friendly messages, and [happy kaomoji](/kaomoji/happy.html) cover smiles, cheers, and good news. For affection, try [love kaomoji and heart emoticons](/kaomoji/love.html). Feeling low? [Sad kaomoji](/kaomoji/sad.html) have tears and sighs, and [angry faces](/kaomoji/angry.html) cover frustration and pouts.

Looking for the classics? Copy the [shrug emoticon](/kaomoji/shrug.html), the [lenny face](/kaomoji/lenny-face.html), or the [table flip](/kaomoji/table-flip.html), or browse the [meme faces](/kaomoji/meme.html) for the facepalm and more. Fans of decoration will like the [aesthetic kaomoji](/kaomoji/aesthetic.html) with stars, sparkles, and flowers, and animal lovers can browse [cat kaomoji](/kaomoji/cats.html), [bear kaomoji](/kaomoji/bears.html), and [bunny kaomoji](/kaomoji/bunnies.html).

sections.h: Tips for using kaomoji in messages
list: Match the tone. A soft face suits a thank-you, and a bold one suits a joke.
Use one face at a time. A single kaomoji reads clearly, while a long chain can look messy.
Put it at the end of a sentence, or send it alone as a quick reaction.
Keep faces short in places with limited space, like bios and usernames.
Test an unusual face in your app first, since a few symbols may look different on some devices.

sections.h: Why plain-text faces still work so well
sections.p: Kaomoji need no app, no keyboard download, and no special font. You copy them, paste them, and they work in chats, comments, emails, notes, and documents. They can also say more than a single emoji, since a face can include arms, sparkles, and small objects. Our guide on [how to copy and paste kaomoji](/how-to-copy-and-paste-kaomoji.html) shows the steps for iPhone, Android, Windows, and Mac.

Kaomoji are text faces, and emoji are pictures. We have both. Start with the [emoji copy and paste](/emoji-copy-and-paste.html) page, or go straight to [love and heart emoji](/emoji/love-hearts.html), [crying and sad emoji](/emoji/crying-sad.html), [happy and laughing emoji](/emoji/happy-smile.html), [cute and aesthetic emoji](/emoji/cute-aesthetic.html), or [cat emoji](/emoji/cat.html). For feelings like anger, tiredness, shock, and doubt, see the [angry](/emoji/angry.html), [tired](/emoji/tired-sleepy.html), [shocked](/emoji/shocked-scared.html), and [thinking](/emoji/thinking-confused.html) emoji pages, or the [slang emoji](/emoji/slang-meme.html) meanings.

Want to go deeper? Read [what is kaomoji](/what-is-kaomoji.html) for the meaning and history, [Japanese emoticons explained](/japanese-emoticons.html) for how they compare with other text faces, and [kaomoji symbols](/kaomoji-symbols.html) for the characters behind every face. To use them in apps, see [kaomoji for Discord, Instagram, and TikTok](/kaomoji-for-discord-instagram-tiktok.html). Want something unique? Make your own with the [kaomoji generator](/kaomoji-generator.html).
